utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Jusic. May I remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Jusic. I'm Vladimir Petrovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. I represent General Strugar, and I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to some of the things you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm honoured to have met you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, tell me, yesterday towards the end of the examination-in-chief, you said that you can hardly wait for the trial to continue and for you to appear before the Trial Chamber yet again this morning. My question is how come? How come that you have this burning wish to do so?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I wish to return to my Dubrovnik as soon as possible. That is my only wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday your lawyers too. Who are your lawyers here? Can you distinguish between the parties involved in these proceedings? Am I your lawyer? Is the other side your -- are they your lawyers, or have you come here to tell the truth as a witness?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came here to tell the truth about what happened in Dubrovnik in 1991 and the years that followed. I'm not hampered by any lawyers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said yesterday that in 1990, if I understood you correctly, you came to Dubrovnik from Zagreb. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that that same year, 1990, you felt that there were some things that were going on and that your town needed you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, what was it that was happening in 1990 at all in the former SFRY to the best of your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The newspapers were full of provocations. The newspapers were full, especially Belgrade newspapers. I can even give you the names of the journalists who wrote false things, that something strange was happening. I did not see that either in Zagreb or in Dubrovnik. Dubrovnik is my hometown. All of my music has to do with Dubrovnik. I simply had to be there. I feel there the best, and I feel close to my town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that the newspapers were full of provocations.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was your view then, in 1990, regarding the victory of a nationalist party in the elections in Croatia, the party of Franjo Tudjman? At that time, you were considered to be a Yugoslav-oriented person. So what was your view regarding the fact that a predominantly nationalist party came to power in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you said. I did not feel that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was this new government like? What is your assessment of this government that was elected into office in May 1990 in Croatia, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a government that was elated, full of optimism that things would move for the better, that we in Dubrovnik and throughout Croatia would finally get the money that we earn, that this money will not go, for example, to Belgrade. And then when we are supposed to do something for ourselves, we literally had to beg in order to be able to build something for ourselves, part of a road, part of a coastline, a building, whatever. This was a generally known thing. And the time had come for us to get rid of that burden. The people of Dubrovnik are very hard working. They want to have what they earned made available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So was that your political view in 1990, that Yugoslavia should be dismantled at all costs?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am at all costs a composer. I am not burdened by politics at all. The only thing that I feel strongly about is justice. I worked a lot, and I was never appropriately remunerated for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you not appropriately remunerated because somebody in Belgrade seized part of your fees or somebody took something away from you that belonged to you?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us clarify something straight away, because I feel that you are leading me somewhere where I don't feel comfortable. I have to tell you that I have a lot of friends in Belgrade. I still have a lot of friends in Belgrade. These friends followed my fate in Dubrovnik. They called me, they helped me in a way, at least in verbal terms, but I needed that. So I don't think that it is those people who attacked me. I was attacked by some kind of army that I used to believe in too. They attacked me all of a sudden, unannounced, and unnecessarily so, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, if possible, to focus on my questions. We started this discussion by my asking you whether you thought then that Yugoslavia should be dismantled at all costs, and your answer to that was, "I'm a composer." But I'm asking you as a person who thinks, as a person who certainly has a view of his own, was that your political position? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't say that to me, yes or no. I want to tell you exactly what I think. The newspapers were full then, and everybody was writing about the fact that we should part our ways peacefully. We are civilised people. As you say, I'm a composer. You're a lawyer, and just as we're discussing things here, I thought that we would discuss things, shake hands, go our separate ways, and that was my position then. And I don't think that it is necessary for you to put words into my mouth that I was thinking in political terms. I was not. I'm not interested in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the fact that you worked for TV Yutel, too, what kind of a television was it? What was the programme orientation of that TV station?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not work for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to put the question, and the question has to be interpreted as well, so could you please wait. Who established Yutel, and who had decisive influence over the editorial policies of that TV station? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I answer now? I did not have any association with Yutel television. I spoke for them just as I spoke for the German television ZDF and for French television and for TV Portugal. I'm not interested. In the summer of 1991, they wanted to make a portrait of mine, my portrait as an artist. I was not interested in who was in charge of that. They had announced themselves, just like many other TV stations did who came to Dubrovnik and to my house. They made a TV programme, about 15 or 20 minutes. This was an artistic portrait of mine. So that's the only thing I know about them, and this is the only dealing I had to do with them. And I think that there was a journalist there, a cameraman, and a secretary. That was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what was this that you said to us yesterday that you carried recordings to the Libertas Hotel and that you are the first person to have sent the truth about Dubrovnik to the world? You told us about that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not quite understand what I was saying. Now I'm going to repeat what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that in the autumn of 1991, I was called by these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people who had done this portrait of mine. They knew where I lived, and they know that I can see Dubrovnik and the panorama of all of Dubrovnik, and they said: "Please give us some information now. In Belgrade they are saying that you are burning tyres, and Zagreb says that you were attacked. Where is the truth?" And the only thing I said: "I'm going to tell you the truth now. A shell fell on St. Ivan's fortress, and also Peskarija, the harbour." That's the only thing I said. I said there were no tyres burning too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you do that? How many times did they call you? How many times did you send them reports, if this can be called a report?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Call it what you will. Once, one single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, yesterday you mentioned that you went to the Libertas Hotel where Croatian television had its offices. What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cared about this truth reaching out to the world. Many journalists asked me to give this. However, I did not know these people. I just happened to see them in Dubrovnik. I gave this to the national TV station, Croatian television from Zagreb in the area of Dubrovnik, that is. I didn't give them everything. I gave them what I had on that day. I did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end because counsel spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us be more specific. I believe that you cannot remember very specifically, though, but what did you give them? How many times did you give it to them? When did you give it to them?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once. Once. And this film was never shown on television because this is what the situation was. Below the town of Dubrovnik, there were a few gunboats. They were moving about all the time. And at one point in time, a yacht appeared. I saw that it was a German yacht. I saw the flag, and it was torpedoed, and it simply disappeared from the horizon. I gave them that cassette. I never saw it again. It was a unique recording. I never got it back. So that was once. And the second time is what we watched yesterday. So it was twice, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why was this dramatic recording not shown, the one that was torpedoed by a Yugoslav navy ship, as you say?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. That is beyond me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us yesterday that all world televisions broadcast your recordings; CNN, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and this is what I got from Croatian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But let us make a distinction. What was it that you gave to them, what was it that they received, and what was broadcast? You said it was on two occasions. On the first occasion you gave them this recording of the torpedoed ship which was lost and was never aired; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it on television. You have to bear in mind we didn't have electricity in Dubrovnik for 157 days, and so we couldn't watch television. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did you give the second material?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment it happened. For instance, if this took place on the 6th and the 7th, it was on the 8th of that month that I gave it to them because it was very important for me that the truth should begin -- be spread on that same day because people were inquiring, "Are you being attacked?" People called me by phone. Friends called me from Belgrade. Is this possible? Is this is not possible? They were very concerned about my fate and my state of health. So we were getting these inquiries all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please. So this was on the 7th, the 8th, and the 9th that you took these tapes to them; right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I took them personally to them and they had them re-recorded and then I took them back because I wanted to make sure that I would have them, I wouldn't have the same experience as with the yacht recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was your experience with the yacht tape since you don't know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never found out that it was broadcast, so I would never let it out of my hands any more. So I just kept them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what was the first time when you re-recorded these tapes of yours?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minute it happened or a couple of days after the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you do this re-recording?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Libertas Hotel, in a cellar. There was a small studio there, a makeshift affair, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Whose studio was this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was a shooting at the studio, the real studio of the Croatian television, they took what they could away, and they set up this makeshift studio, and that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this is what you used a couple of days after this event in December?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to do it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how was it possible that you did this at the Libertas Hotel on the 6th, 7th, and 8th of December when it is well -- a well-known fact that the Hotel Libertas burned down?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, a second ago I told you that this took place in the cellar. The hotel building was devastated, the large reception hall, the lobby existed no longer. These were ruins. It was burnt down. There was no elevator. We went down into the cellar on foot, taking the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the Hotel Libertas did not burn down on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was devastated. It was demolished. It burned down. There was a fire brigade. You keep asking me about the 6th of December. I cannot tell you with precision. Perhaps it may have been before. There is a plaque at the hotel to honour the memory of the people who got killed so please don't try to confuse me by these exact days or minutes. I cannot remember that with precision, but it was then, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So at any rate, when did you go to the Hotel Libertas to make these copies? At the time when you went to make these copies, it hadn't been burnt down, it was intact.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had burnt down. There was just the skeleton of the hotel that was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, where down? To -- what was there below the Hotel Libertas that you went to?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some big corridors, some sort of a room, a large conference room but without anything in it. There were no glasses, no viewers [as interpreted] in it. There was nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you assert that the studio of Croatian television at that time was at the Libertas Hotel which had burnt down.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the cellars, in the basement, in some corridors of the hotel. This is your position?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this was not a studio in normal terms. These were two or three appliances, apparatus. It was not a real studio. You know what a real studio looks like, more or less like this courtroom. It is a huge room. This was just a small room. It was a makeshift affair because they normally had a studio up there at Boninovo, the real TV studio, which still is there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this makeshift studio was there after the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was there so as to be safe and in a place that no shell could reach and had no reason to target, a place that no one had any reason to target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if there was no electricity, how were you able to work in that basement?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the hotels had some generating sets. For instance, the Excelsior Hotel next to us, they had electricity. You could hear sounds coming from it as well as from the Hotel Argentina, which also had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a set. The Revelin Fort also had a generating set, and some of them had these small Yamaha generating sets, and they provided electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So after the fire of the 6th of December, in this hotel there remained an intact electrical installation and a generating set which was supplying electricity to this makeshift studio. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't so. We didn't have electricity in the entire hotel, it was just in that part, the basement. There was a swimming pool on the top floor of the hotel, the gym. There was no electricity. The installations were down. We just had these small makeshift affairs, generating sets which could perhaps help you light a bulb or two, a miniature thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how did you get into the hotel? And if I'm not wrong, one reaches the hotel from up, gets into the hotel from above. And how did you enter the hotel in this upper storey? The entrance to the hotel had been demolished. How did you get into the hotel? What route did you take?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, as you said, I had to creep into the hotel. If the lobby was above there, it was all in glass and it existed no more, so one had to actually creep into the hotel, and that is a proper way of putting it. Exactly. That's how I got in, creeping into the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any other people creep into the hotel getting into it and out of it in that way?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody else. When I came there, a young man was waiting for me after I had crept into the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who was this young man? Who did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belong to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was he doing there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some sort of a technician there in the TV studio.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you get in touch with this young man at all? The telephones were down, there was no electricity; how did this whole thing come about at all?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are saying, that there was no telephone connection, at sometimes the telephones did work. People would call you via radio stations, saying that they had lost trace of their kin or the people in their family had been killed, and so on and so forth, so that telephones sometimes did work in this way. And Radio Dubrovnik also had a generating set, and it was also airing its programmes using this set.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who else was there when you were copying these things?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This lad and another one. So there were two young men about 30 years old. They are young in relation to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know them from before? What are their names?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One is Vedran Benic. He is an editor now, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the other one?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. We'll go back to that a bit later. Were you -- did you regret the fact that the SFRY was no more?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regretted the way in which things could happen, and I'm thinking, for instance, about Czechoslovakia where they nicely sat down and agreed and said we would remain friends and let's move on. So nobody -- none of us expected this -- this punch in the belly, this surprise, this thing that we all experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you personally feel that Belgrade was ripping you off, that your money was going to Belgrade? Was this your conviction as well?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look here -- well, I don't know what to reply to that. I didn't come -- I didn't go to Belgrade much, and my relations with the people there were very correct. Not only business relations but also friendly relations. Still today I have friends there, and it is my contention that it wasn't exactly Belgrade that attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, Mr. Jusic, about the attack. What I'm asking you about is the time --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you're asking me. I'll finish. I'm a composer. Okay. So my songs listened to in Belgrade, Zagreb, Ljubljana, et cetera, and all this forms which are written in that connection go to Belgrade and there they actually determine how much goes in terms of remuneration to a certain composer. So since I didn't have a team of lawyers to follow this, I couldn't actually monitor this. But this was a general opinion, and it was always in the papers, and they always indicated some specific date, but this is a general information in the papers that this was happening. I cannot reply to the effect that I was personally ripped off or whether I was or wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, so it was in Belgrade that actually summed up how much of your particular songs were aired, in which particular station or situation. So you said it was in that they would sum up the broadcasting times of your music in different places. So what significance is the fact that this was done in Belgrade if it was done properly? If it wasn't done properly, does that mean you were ripped off by someone in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, I'll give you an example. For example, my music was broadcast throughout the world and this was done through an European agency which is called G-E-M-A, Gema, and the money, the proceeds and the information about the broadcasting would go to Belgrade, to the capital. So for instance now it's the year 2004. In 2004, I'm receiving money which I earned in 2001, with a three-year delay, in other words. Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You're telling me Belgrade is to blame for this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is just where the money went. You are putting words into my mouth. I'm just giving you a concrete example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now I suppose this is much better. Things have improved because the money is now in Zagreb and no one is touching your money in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't ask me that. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not putting to you an indecent question.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was indecent. But if you so wish I can give you an answer to that question as well, but there is no need. I have not put the blame at Belgrade's door, which you're trying to put into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you then think that this country should be dismantled?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never thought that. I never said that. I thought that we should actually part in a civilised way. This is the general opinion in Croatia. We will be to -- deal with this together with Serbia, with Montenegro, and everyone will keep their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To sum this up, to recapitulate, so it was Belgrade that was ripping Dubrovnik off and actually seizing the results of its work, including the work of your work.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're constantly putting in my mouth things which I didn't say, and please tell me what is it that you want me to say to you. I never mentioned any rip-offs. This was a general view. It was a generally known thing. It was common knowledge. It was something which was written about in the papers daily, in Serbia, Croatia, Montenegrin papers, this was not something I made up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was it a generally held belief or was it the truth? Please --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please let me finish. Was it a generally held belief or was it true that the results of the labour of Dubrovnik and Croatia were appropriated by someone in Belgrade? Was it the generally held belief or was it the truth?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I didn't have those papers in my hands. It was a general truth. That was precisely the reason why we should have parted amicably, because we all know that the Serbian people are hard working, that the Croatian people are hard working, and why, then, did we have to go through all that? We could have negotiated. And I can see that the two of us would have had a very nicely negotiated, amicable settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But perhaps we could have peacefully remained together.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, definitely. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the political situation in Croatia was exacerbating, which is what you say a few times in your statement. Now, tell me, what were the specific manifestations of this deterioration of the situation in Croatia? What was actually happening?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be brief so we can go home as early as possible and transact our business.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, in Dubrovnik, Nin was a favourite magazine which -- in which wrote many famous journalists and some acquaintances, and in fact friends of mine. For instance, there was a journalist by the name of Momo Kapor who wrote this article I believe in the fall of 1990. He wrote about Dubrovnik where he said Croatians are throwing little children into the air, smashing their heads against the concrete, ripping off parts of their bodies. So this provoked general shock in Dubrovnik, general shock. The very idea that a person who had been a friend of the people of Dubrovnik, who came to Dubrovnik at least two times a year, was saying such things. What does this tell us? This tells us that someone was trying to incite, ignite a fire that no one needed. Then there was this second journalist. I remember this very vividly because there was general consternation. People were really concerned that someone could write things like that. For instance, in 1991 when Dubrovnik was -- and this was in 1991 when Dubrovnik was full of tourists and it seems to me at that took place a year before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this the most dramatic thing that happened in Croatia in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what could be more dramatic than that, because those people are my friends. The Serbs are. Jews are my friends. Catholics are my friends. I had an Orthodox musician in my band. He stayed with my band for 20 or 30 years. All this only goes to show that Dubrovnik was absolutely not encumbered by this sort of thing. But it was certainly burdened by such falsehoods as this article by Momo Kapor which I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you read this article?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I even left it -- I deposited it somewhere for posterity to be able to show it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, were there any armed conflicts there? In addition to this article that you have been describing, did people -- were people getting killed? What was happening? Was there something more drastic, more dramatic than the article by Momo Kapor?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were peacefully enjoying ourselves at the beach and enjoying the beauties of our city. People were bringing the fruit of their labour to the Konavle market. The people, the sailors from the coastal folk living there, and that's how we went about our normal business. There were no armed conflicts, there were no attacks, there were no uniforms, no weapons, nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What period are you referring to? When was this happening when you were peacefully bathing at the beach and there were no armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period you asked me about, 1990, 1991 until September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the only thing which actually unsettled you in this entire period was this article by Momo Kapor. Everything else was all right in Dubrovnik, in Croatia, in Yugoslavia. Everything else was okay?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are relating me to Momo Kapor. There was countless such articles. This was the first one, and it was so unpleasant and so glaringly so, but there were other articles as well of that type. And then in the summer of 1991, there were some aircraft that were flying over the Stradun, and I know that some people were writing about how this was affecting the foundations of the Old City which were shaking, and already at that time there were some hints of what would come. It is really not pleasant for me to have a plane flying over my head, breaking the sound walls. And this was in 1991. I just remembered that this happened in that year. So don't just ask me about me about Momo Kapor. Others also wrote things like that. Tijanic, for instance, and all these other journalists whom we all well liked. They were all well-liked. These were -- but then we were asking ourselves, what kind of a people were they when they could write such things?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any troops in Dubrovnik at any time?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think the army was in Dubrovnik until 1980 when Dubrovnik was declared a protected city. The Yugoslav army was at Gruz and was transferred to Trebinje. Perhaps it was prior to 1980, but after that there were no troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So tell me. This was probably the proclamation of the city as protected UNESCO city. One of the conditions for that was to transfer the garrison from the city to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I remember it was one of the requirements to be filled for that. And it was good for Dubrovnik as a tourist city. Why would you want to have soldiers roaming about a city, and troops? It was generally nothing apart from the fact that Trebinje is quite near. It's 20 minutes away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I can imagine how shocked you were when in the city of Dubrovnik you saw members of the Croatian army of the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not shocked at all because this didn't happen. You are imputing the things to me again. I never saw troops in town, not the Guard, not the other formations you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that later. You said yesterday, "I had to defend my town." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you view this role of yours? How is this that a composer can defend his town? What did you do, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a practical answer. People were scattered about in different shelters. I'll give you the names of a few shelters where I organised some programmes: St. Ivan, Revelin, Minceta, then the Franciscan cloister. I organised a kind of programme every day there for some singing to be going on, for the children to be cheered up. There were no political speeches or any such thing. That was my mission. I wrote quite a few songs precisely then, during the war. One was even proclaimed the most patriotic song after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you wrote patriotic songs for the homeland, to raise the morale of the population.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. These were not warrior songs. This was not a call to rebellion, no. Look, we are actually talking about me, and they -- and people say that when guns shoot, the muses fall silent, and I wanted it to be the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did all the musicians of Dubrovnik take such a stand in this situation?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who stayed behind, because many left in order to make a living elsewhere. But I stayed and many people stayed. The symphony orchestra was still there, then also the children's choir that I was in charge of, then also there were smaller ensembles, then Tereza Kesovija remained in Dubrovnik, and she sang often. By the way, her house, her new villa in Konavle, was razed to the ground. And that's the kind of thing that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody call you up then? How old were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was pretty old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't look that way.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was pretty old.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody call you up, though?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no call-up for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any call-ups for other musicians?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are trying to saddle me with the military all the time. I did not see any call-up papers, any such thing. I don't know. I don't know. I'm going to answer all your questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask the speakers to slow down and not to overlap each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you continue almost to argue with the witness as he's trying to answer. Could you observe the guidance you gave to the witness at the beginning and wait until he's finished and the interpretation is finished before carrying on. And you, sir, will remember that guidance that was given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, I'm going to put some questions to you, those that are allowed by the Trial Chamber. If the Trial Chamber does not allow any of my questions, then the situation is quite different, of course. However, if the Trial Chamber allows these questions, then please answer my questions by saying, "I know," "I don't know," "I did see," "I did not see." That's no problem whatsoever. If you never saw a Croat soldier in town, you're going to tell me, "I never saw one in town," and that will be the end of that part of our conversation. I'm going to put questions to you as I deem necessary in the best interests of my client in accordance with the Rules of this Tribunal. So my question to you was: Were there any musicians who were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there general mobilisation in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Dubrovnik a defended town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a defended town only through the will of its people. I remember once when this army, the aggressor, was in a position to enter the town with an orchestra. Perhaps I could put it that way. However, the people said that they would act as they did in the medieval times, that from their windows they would pour hot oil on the invaders. That's the only thing I heard of. Old women were saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the people of Dubrovnik prepare anything else to deal with the aggressor except for this hot oil?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything else, perhaps, any other of these ancient methods of defence; for example, tar and setting fires and things like that? Any such thing?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, perhaps I should explain some things. You could have a million dollars in your pocket, but we were dreaming of seeing a single apple or a single carrot, because the enemy had burned everything down. So we could not really be bothered by things like those that you are proposing right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody take care of the defence of Dubrovnik? I mean, this hot oil, the tar and everything else, did anybody organise any such thing?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you're saying tar and I didn't say tar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Hot oil, then.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I'm talking to you about the Old Town within the Old City walls. That is where I walked about from my apartment, and I swore that I would tell the truth. Within the Old City walls, there was no such thing like what you are aiming at. So please go ahead and put your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me what is it that I'm aiming at. What do I find -- what am I trying to get at?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say oil and you add tar, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was it that you moved about the town of Dubrovnik at the time that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the Franciscan cloister and then the building of the festival and then the concert at the cathedral. We did not really have much space. We were all moving within, say, a single kilometre or a kilometre and a half. I really missed my walking, so then I walked by the city walls so that the enemy would not see me from Zarkovica. I went jogging, for instance. But there weren't any meeting places where people would meet up. I would go to see my friends at St. Ivan, at the aquarium or at Fort Revelin, places like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say that you could move for about a kilometre and a half from your house which is above the Excelsior Hotel. In which direction?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the Old City walls and then by the houses, by the buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between your apartment and the Old City walls?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say 700, 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what is the distance between your apartment and the Libertas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: One kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In order to reach your apartment -- to reach Libertas from your apartment, where would you did?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd go through town. I'd go to Pile. You know what the layout is, then I would go up to Put Ivana Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ante Starcevic.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Starcevic. Now I see that you do know about this. And then Libertas is there near the cemetery. There were some periods when there were no alerts. You know, we weren't really under sirens all the time. We already learned what the system was, and that remained a mystery to me; how did they know that the attack had ended?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, October, November, and December, these three months, how much of this time did you spend in a shelter or wherever you were hiding when the attack would start?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this inner feeling of protest. I did not want to go to shelters. I went to a shelter only one single time. I went to a shelter which is near my apartment building. It was called the atomic shelter. That was one of the bad days. My apartment faces Dubrovnik and the sea, and I did my composing then. As a matter of fact, I composed an oratorium then, which is called The Truth -- The Truth of a Free -- About a Free Town. And I also wrote this in Latin, "De Civitate Libertatis Veritas." I did this based on the text written by a bishop, and it was performed later on. I would like to have that oratorium performed in Belgrade too. That is my wish, and I hope that it will be performed in Belgrade some day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who wrote the lyrics, the verses?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Zelimir Puljic and poet Luka Paljetak. And the choir of the Split Opera sang, and the soloist was Ruza Pospis-Baldani, and the Dubrovnik Symphony Orchestra performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the performance took place on the 6th of December, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what was the situation like in Dubrovnik at that time? You were either very brave or it was not dangerous. I don't know what else one could infer.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you just now that perhaps I was brave to the point of madness. I said that to you, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go -- where else did you go within the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijeko.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I say the town of Dubrovnik, I mean --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Old City walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us clarify one thing: When I say the town of Dubrovnik, I'm referring to the town, and when I say the Old Town, then I mean what is within the Old City walls. So my question is where else did you move about in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly within the Old Town. And sometimes, when there would be a lull for a few days, then I would go to Lapad. I would go for a walk to Lapad and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far away is that? From your house, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You went to Lapad. Could you mention a few hotels in the Bay of Lapad?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Park, Adriatic, Vis I, Vis II. That would be about it. I didn't spend much time in Lapad. But Babin Kuk is not Lapad, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in these hotels?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, refugees from Konavle, Primorje, from the places where people were expelled from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself see them there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, lots of them. They were walking around when I came there. They were in tatters because they couldn't take anything from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know where Hotel Zagreb is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also in Lapad somewhere. I -- I think it's -- it's on the main road, where the tram goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see refugees at that hotel too?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I ever passed that hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But as you were walking about town, was there a specific reason why you didn't pass that particular hotel? After all, it's spectacularly sited. It's nice to walk around.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me a hand with this, please. Where exactly is the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the hotel is. I think it's on the main promenade, where the tram used to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know what there was at that hotel? You don't even seem to know that it exists.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that hotel. I know that it existed but I don't know what was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As you walked around, as you walked from the Excelsior Hotel, which is in the east, through the Old Town, through all the main streets leading to the town's western section, through the Lapad Bay - you walked on and on for kilometres - did you ever come across any persons wearing uniforms, carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the regular police forces. I'm not sure why they were there or in what capacity. It was some sort of a grey, a greyish uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Vila Rasica is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's further up on that slope to the left as you head for Lapad, or around there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you walk by that building?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not a place you'd pass on your way anywhere because the road descends steeply from there and the house is further up the slope. It was some sort of a youth association, I believe, earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about wartime? What was based at that building?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the Belvedere Hotel? Were there refugees there too?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Belvedere Hotel is a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you just please answer my question. Were there any refugees at the Belvedere Hotel? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Belvedere Hotel had burned down and it wasn't possible to put anyone up there, so I can't say yes or no. It simply wasn't like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did the Belvedere Hotel burn down?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It burnt down because a gunboat had arrived one morning, a ship with a gun mounted, and it came within a hundred metres from the hotel itself, and it fired at all the hotel's windows, and it went on firing until the whole thing burnt down. Therefore, all you can see today is the skeleton of what used to be a hotel. Only the outer walls. So what this shows is that anyone who had a weapon could fire at the hotel. They could even have thrown stones at the hotel and shattered the windows. Only a madman would have done something like that. The hotel burned down, therefore no chance anyone could have been there. You know, people are not birds; they can't live on walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit rich of you to ask me about the dates. It was a long time ago. I didn't keep track of the dates and hour -- and hours of the day. It was back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell me -- I'm not specifically asking about the date but could you just give me the month; October, November, December, early on in the month, late in the month, beginning of 1991 or 1992? Just roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I remember it, it was before the 6th of December. I was watching from my window, and this gunboat was just firing away mercilessly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you actually see the Hotel Belvedere from your window?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the surrounding area around the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the boat arrive within a hundred metres. It was a gunboat. I'm not sure, it had some letters and numbers on it. 134, I believe. And then it started just firing away at the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And there were refugees inside the hotel; right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. The refugees fled west to the Babin Kuk area and thereabouts. As far as I know, there were no refugees in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So before the hotel was fired on, who had stayed there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hotel that was open for the whole summer just before in 1991. It was a five-star hotel, so it was quite a posh hotel, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there were tourists there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then the hotel was fired at and the tourists left?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was. When the autumn was under way, ships arrived all around Dubrovnik at a mile or two outside Dubrovnik. Warships, so obviously it was clear to everyone that they should just leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you give a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean those who came to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they caution you that you were supposed to tell the truth, that you were supposed to tell everything you knew about what they were asking you about?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a friendly interview. It wasn't necessary for anyone to caution me about my duty to tell the truth. It's just that you want me to say something different from what I'm saying now but there's no way I can do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you gave that statement, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll read out to you paragraph 16 of your statement now, where you state the following: "By November 1991, the whole area of Dubrovnik was occupied and hotels were full of refugees. Later on, the aggressors (Serbs, Montenegrins, JNA) attacked these hotels as well. These hotels are: Hotel Kompas, Excelsior, Belvedere, and Libertas." Does this not seem to indicate that there were refugees at the Belvedere Hotel too? Isn't that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no refugees there, but there were refugees in all these other hotels. I just listed several hotels like that. We were talking about the summer, which is when I had to leave my yacht behind, and I came there to talk to them. Perhaps my attitude was slightly naive too. So I referred to the Belvedere Hotel, but I don't think it has any specific meaning in this context. I can specify now that there were no refugees at the time at the Belvedere Hotel because it was impossible for anyone to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, why weren't refugees at the Belvedere Hotel? It was closest to the Konavle area, it would have been only natural for the refugees to go there and not any further off.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you now that the hotel had burned down. It was the closest hotel but there were boats outside the hotel. No one would have been foolish to go there seeing that the boats were that close.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I think my question to you is specific enough. By the time --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no refugees at the Belvedere Hotel, and that's my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me who was there at the Belvedere Hotel.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very far from where I live, about a kilometre. There was no chance for anyone to walk that far. Just opposite the house there is a bunker with a machine-gun. Whenever I walked down the street, someone was firing at me. I had to crawl on all fours. There used to be Yugoslav flag down there for a while, and even the Serbian flag. They often spoke to us from up there. That's how close they were. We could actually hear their voices. I don't know who specifically was there but it would have been impossible for anyone to stay at the hotel since the hotel had burned down, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know who was at the hotel at the time.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know when the hotel burned down specifically.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're trying to wrong foot me all the time. I told you this was probably before the 6th. It may even have been in November. I really can't remember the specific date, but the way I remember it now --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Reading further on in your statement, paragraph 16 also, at the beginning of that paragraph - I'm not reading the whole thing again but I believe my colleague Kaufman will stand up and object if I get anything wrong - it says, "By November 1991..." and then whatever happened by November 1991, and then it continued. "The Libertas Hotel was completely destroyed and certain firemen were killed there." That's by November. And then further on: "One day, a gunboat attacked the Belvedere Hotel and opened fire on it, which proves that the Croatians had no weapons to respond to these attacks."

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said awhile ago, the very same thing I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So now, sir, please tell me, how is that proof that the Croats had no weapons to respond to the attack? How can one logically arrive at this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my conclusion was that the gunboat was so close that you could have hit it with a glass if you threw a glass at it. So probably someone would have fired at it if there had been any weapons to fire by. So that was the logic that led me to assume that the Croats had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, aren't you perhaps phrasing this in a way that's slightly liberal or inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps this is an example of liberal phrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Srdj is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just behind me. Just behind where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, on Srdj there is a very important monument of culture, the Imperijal Fort, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Imperijal Fort, which had been built by Napoleon's forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This fort was a protected monument of culture, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't as important as the Old Town itself, but this building, too, marked a time of aggression, when Napoleon and his forces attacked the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the war, was it used for cultural purposes?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just next to the fortress there is a funicular which had also been demolished. So before the war, we used to take this funicular to go up the mountain, and at the fort there was a disco.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any concerts that were organised there, art exhibitions?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a disco. It was a very popular haunt for the people of Dubrovnik. It was a famous club. Just between the cable car and the fortress, where the cross was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you again, were there any art exhibition or concerts being held at the Imperijal Fort?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anything that happens in a disco. I'm not sure that can be considered a concert. Not a concert of classical music. But there were different things going on there, so there may as well have been concerts too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the Imperijal Fort, did you see the sign, the UNESCO sign marking it off as a monument of culture, as world heritage at the time?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, not that I could see from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why wasn't that particular monument of culture marked in a proper way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. I'm not sure this witness is qualified to comment on matters of legal import.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir, who was at Srdj at that time in October, November, and December?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go up there myself so I can't say who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the disco open at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, because the cable car had been demolished, destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was possible to go up there without the cable car, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, did people go up there to Srdj or not?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see that from where I was, from where my flat is. From inside Dubrovnik itself you can't see the path going up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come you were weren't able to see it? You not only saw it, you actually recorded it. In the footage you recorded, there are several sequences showing the fort.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But from the town itself, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Regardless.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the town itself, but you can't see any people in the footage that I took. I don't know that there were any people there. It just -- if I try to remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So tell me, sir, where is this bunker where the Serb flag was displayed, the one that you saw?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you provide a map, I'll mark it for you on a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the location, please.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's the Excelsior Hotel, and then some ten metres further down is the Lazarina Street, which I take whenever I go home; and in the same direction on top of Mount Srdj there was a bunker, a Yugoslav flag for a while, and then a Serb flag; and they were shouting down from the top of the hill, "Ustasha, we're coming down. We're coming for you." It was ridiculous and tragic at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So who was up there? The aggressors, I assume.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the aggressors were at this location I've just described. I think that was the furthest point they reached in the direction of the fort itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But why weren't they inside the fort, then? It was so conveniently located after all; you could see the whole town from it. It was empty. There was a disco there. Anyone would have been free to just walk in and take the fort. Why weren't they there? Why didn't they move in? Perhaps they were there but you don't know.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Isn't this bunker where you saw those people with a Serbian flag equally distant from your flat as the Imperijal Fort?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that position, from my street I can't see the fort itself, but this was exactly in my view. I was -- are you following what I'm saying, sir? I was humiliated there, totally humiliated, because I had to crawl up the street. I had to crawl up the steps, and there were sniper bullets flying around me. And it is by sheer chance that I'm alive here today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Petrovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know many people in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less all of us know each other, at least by sight, and we greet each other. We always wish other people good morning or a good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you contact many people as you were walking about town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In those hard times, what did people talk about?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were talking about where they could find an onion or a carrot to cook some soup. They were wishing they could find a piece of bacon because it was wintertime. All of that is probably meaningless to you but it was of capital importance in Dubrovnik then in terms of survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Those are not unimportant things to me. It is not meaningless, but what I'm interested in is were you talking about this man with the Serbian flag up there at the bunker? What is it that is preventing him from coming down?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to digress now and give you an opinion of my own. For example, I had a transistor radio, a transistor radio, and then I listened to the Montenegrin radio stations. At a given point in time when Dubrovnik was morally disarmed, when people had lost all hope, this Montenegrin radio station was saying that in Dubrovnik there were 6.000 members of the National Guards Corps and Ustashas. I don't know how they could say that. And then I realised that perhaps they were afraid or perhaps somebody wouldn't let them do whatever, but at any rate, this is what I heard with my very own ears. I heard other things too but this is very important. That is very important in terms of why they did not come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So as for the members of the National Guards Corps and the Croatian army, you only know about them from Radio Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You never heard about any such thing in the town of Dubrovnik from this multitude of people you talked to? Didn't you ask anyone? "People, is it possible that there are 6.000 Croatian soldiers here?" Were you interested in checking this information out?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honey, that is ridiculous. We were looking at bread. We were discussing how much bread was sold that day. We were not talking about army, the military, whatever. Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you did not hear or see anyone?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just heard this one from up there saying, "Ustashas, here we come," and I don't really want to use the other words they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jusic. Tell me, do you have any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do. Three brothers and three sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what are your brothers' names?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this really important to you to enter my family matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I can tell you. One is Kemal, the oldest one. The other is Ibrica, and the third one is Mujica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, are all of them law-abiding citizens, honest men?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm proud of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you talking to all of them? Are you on speaking terms with all of them?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have normal contact with Ibrica, Kemal, Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. The other day we all had lunch together at my older brother's place. He gathered us all about 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did your brothers live in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrica was on tour somewhere. In Zagreb, I believe. At any rate, he was not in Dubrovnik. And the other two brothers were in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Ibrica come to Dubrovnik during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him. I heard that he came. I heard that he had a charity concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were Kemal and Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, they live on the other side of town. They both live in Lapad, in Batala Street. So I didn't see them often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what did Kemal and Mujica do during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taking care of their children. One of them also had to repair his house because a shell had hit it, and he had to cover it with plastic sheets, whatever, and the other one was taking care of his children. Apropos of Mujica, his wife is of the Orthodox religion and her father held a high rank in the Yugoslav army. So I think that you're on the wrong track here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why do you think I'm on the wrong truck? In relation to what?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you're trying to get something out of me. I don't know how to put this. I don't know why we're discussing my brothers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's forget about all of this anyway. Tell me, I did not understand one thing. So Kemal's house was hit and Mujica was taking care of his children.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What is the last name of Mujica's wife? What is the family that she comes from?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me a lot now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because of this high-ranking officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this in passing. There is no special reason for it. It's not that important. But I cannot remember now because this was his second marriage -- I mean, it's not that it was, it still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with Kemal in October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as possible. Actually, the subjects discussed were, "What are you eating? Have you got any canned food?" And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact about Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely because we could not get up there to Lapad. It was risky. There were sirens all the time and we didn't know when there would be shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you went to Lapad, did you stop by to see Kemal and Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did stop by to see Kemal, yes. I would do that. His house was destroyed and then a neighbour let him use an apartment, so he lived there for a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop by to see Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go to see Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I put a question to you, the other way round? Why am I sitting here? Let's turn the tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not go to see Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, if you are going to see someone, you're supposed to have been invited beforehand, at least that's part of the manners I was taught. We could not see each other, we could not speak, so I didn't want to barge into somebody's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But it is a war. It was a war. He had young children. People did not have enough to eat, so what happened to Mujica, your own brother?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'd speak on the telephone. He could not come to see me, I could not come to see him in Lapad so it wasn't that there was no contact between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask Kemal about Mujica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific. Women, children. He'd go to meet a boat. Friends would send him something. Look, you're trying to raise this all up to a high level, and people were desperate to get something for their children, at least, to try to obtain, say, gas, because there was no electricity, and there was no water, and gas bottles arrived from somewhere else and then they cost a fortune. You're asking me about high politics, and we were dreaming about apples, carrots, a slice of bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Mujica perhaps preparing the oil?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, how can you tell me about all these things? I mentioned this in connection with the city walls. Your Honour. Your Honour. Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? May I address you, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea if we just called a halt now. I'm going to say a few words to Mr. Petrovic, and then after the break, if you think you need to address me, yes, but you listen to what happens now first. Mr. Petrovic, I've allowed this cross-examination to go on for a considerable time in the expectation that you would come to some matter that really was important over each line that you've pursued. I haven't yet found that you have done that. Certainly, for example, not about the family of the witness. I mention that because we're now going to have a break, and I hope that you will be able to focus your questions more clearly on matters that are directly pertinent to the defence when we return. Now, there's something you would like to say before we break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. I'm asking the distinguished gentleman about his brother Mujica because of Mr. Mujica's role in everything that we are talking about, and that is the very core of the matter, the very core of the Defence case in relation to what was happening in Dubrovnik in 1991. Your Honours, this was a member of the Croatian army. He took part in many operations in the area of the town of Dubrovnik. This is a man who took up arms near the Old Town of Dubrovnik itself. He gave a statement to that effect to the investigators of this Tribunal, and as you can see, the witness has been very evasive, and he has been trying to dodge all questions in this respect. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that explanation, Mr. Petrovic. As you will appreciate, the Chamber has no present knowledge of that and no --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- emerged to us from what you were questioning. So if there is a particular point to make about the brother, I'd suggest you get to it and make the point when we resume. We will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think in view of what happened just before the break, we might proceed with questioning. Were you content that we were alert to your concern, Mr. Jusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not concerned at all. The only thing I failed to comprehend -- of course, this is a very likable manner in which Mr. Petrovic is pursuing his line of questioning, always reverting to some answer that I had already provided, but when he refers to it, he always adds something to it in order to wrong foot me, so that this would be reflected in the transcript. So I will kindly ask him not to revert to questions that I've already given answers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, and we are conscious of those matters, and we are alert to them as well. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, can we go on?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You saw your brother for the last time a couple of days ago at the place of your oldest brother Kemal?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
