utterances.text: We often met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell your brothers where you were going and where you had been a couple of days before that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in all the Croatian papers, in fact, that I was going to The Hague to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about this with Mujica as well?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, before the break you told us that you had seen all of your brothers immediately prior to your departure for The Hague, including Kemal.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were together about a month ago, but not immediately prior to my departure, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And a month ago did you tell Mujica that you were going to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have read it in the papers. There was no need for me to specifically talk about it, because at that time I hadn't been aware of this other summons. The dates hadn't been fixed yet. I was not sure when I would be going.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Mujica ever tell you that he had given a statement for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him that you had talked with a gentleman from the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Jusic, why are you hiding from this Trial Chamber the fact that your brother was a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear about it, from you. If he was a member, then I really have only admiration for him for defending his children and his homeland, and I am even more proud of him as of this moment when you said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, for how long was he a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? It would be nice if you call him --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has already said that he didn't know his brother was a member of the Croatian army until he appeared in The Hague. So for Mr. Petrovic to then go and ask the witness for how long was he a member of the Croatian army seems to be not a very logical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Kaufman, but I think we can see that Mr. Jusic is well capable of taking care of those matters. Otherwise, we would have interfered earlier and ensured there was no misleading. But you will note the point again, Mr. Petrovic. It's a further example of the style of questioning about which Mr. Jusic is validly complaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the cars on the parking lot behind the Old Town were set on fire in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a shell which landed, I believe, on the 6th, and this is a place which can be seen from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were other cars that were set on fire. In Ploce, in other places. And the windows of most had been shattered. And they were set on fire. I know that a neighbour of mine had a Chrysler, and he took it to a parking lot somewhere near the town and a shell landed directly under his car that was at the Ploce Gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the parking lot next to the Old Town ramparts is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. I was born there. There was a small soccer field there, and I used to play there. I know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this parking lot is directly abutting the northern wall?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to the door which we call Buza.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your brother and his unit opened fire on the 6th of December from that parking lot?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but every honour to him if he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your brother actually caused the -- these cars to be set on fire by consciously provoking units of the JNA to open fire at this parking lot where he was on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think that's pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would at this moment request perhaps Mr. Petrovic, so I don't accuse him of misleading the witness with an incorrect reference to Mr. Mujic -- Jusic's statement, for him to refer me to which part of Mujica Jusic's statement he's putting to the witness. I have in front of me page 6 of that statement and I understand the positioning of Mr. Mujica Jusic on that date to be very different. Perhaps Mr. Petrovic could assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 12th of October 1991, your brother --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm waiting for an answer or a submission before you go on with questioning. Are you putting to this witness something from the statement of his brother?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour. Yes. Well, I meant to start at the beginning of that statement and then eventually come to this part which concerns my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just give a page reference and that will enable him to look at it while you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I may be specific, Your Honours, Mr. Petrovic put a question with reference to the 6th of December. That would be the relevant part I'm looking for, the positioning of Mr. Mujica Jusic that provoked the fire on the 6th of December, as Mr. Petrovic put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would ask to go through the statement, and this will be clarified, and in the process you will also be familiarised with the content of the statement, and all these things will be much clearer. I did ask a question with relation to the 6th of December because the witness, in his answer, implied something of the kind, but of course I shall examine the statement thoroughly if you so permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I may be able to reply. I may be able to assist Mr. Petrovic in this matter because I have a completely different positioning from Mr. Mujica Jusic according to his statement on the 6th of December, to be found in page 6 in the third paragraph from the bottom, for Mr. Petrovic's assistance. He said that he was positioned at Solitudo on the Babin Kuk peninsula, which is nowhere near the parking lot of the Old Town, at least from my knowledge of the geography of the area. Now -- assuming that Mr. Petrovic is aware of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: -- I would assume that he would want to correctly put matters to the witness, and furthermore, if he wished to pursue this matter further, to substantiate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But of course, Your Honour, in order to deal with all these quandaries, I will start at the beginning, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Can I indicate that at the moment, the position has been put clearly against you that you had quite misunderstood the statement of the witness's brother and had wrongly put a location with respect to the 6th of December. If you understand that, then we will, of course, allow you to deal with the statement with a view, you say, to showing on what basis you justify your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, gladly. The reason why the Defence will be asking questions in conformity with the statement is the right of the Defence in accordance with Rule 92(H)(i) to present to the witness elements which form the Defence case and for the witness to state his view in regard to such elements which constitute the Defence case. This is the grounds upon which we are asking to pursue this exercise, but if this Chamber deems it necessary, I can elaborate this at some length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let me say, Mr. Petrovic, we certainly appreciate that and applaud that you should do that. The apparent basis upon which you put the question to which Mr. Kaufman objected was a statement of the brother of the witness, and Mr. Kaufman has raised a concern that you have misunderstood that statement and have, therefore, put a question to the witness which is not in accordance with the statement. Quite separately from the statement of the witness, of the witness's brother, it may be the Defence case that his brother was doing certain things on the 6th of December. If it is within the knowledge or control of the witness, he may properly be questioned by you putting your Defence case to him about that point, but at the moment, it's not apparent on what basis this witness would have had knowledge or control of his brother's conduct on the 6th of December or any other day. Now, I mention those things so that you can keep them in your mind as you frame your questions and pursue your line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what is the grounds for my further answers? The grounds is constituted by the fact that the witness repeatedly said that he moved about town, that he had talked to a multitude of people in town, that during these months he kept in touch with his brothers, with both of his brothers, that they talked on the telephone, and that it is only reasonable to assume that this witness, if he knows what was happening to so many other people in the city, also knows what was happening to his own brother Djurmane [phoen]. So this is the basis, Your Honour, for my questions. He's speaking about events. He's familiar with events and people, and it is fully to be expected, Your Honour, that naturally he is perfectly aware of where his younger brother is and what he is doing. So that all this, with the presentation of our case, also has a strong dose of testing the credibility of this witness who obviously does not at all wish to speak about his brother and generally about the participation and engagement of the Croatian army in the period under review, and he is ignoring this, and that is the key to the credibility of this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be a matter for future evidence what is the role of his brother and of the Croatian army, and of course there has been some evidence with respect to that. You certainly, Mr. Petrovic, may be putting your case about that, but it has to be relevant to this witness in some way. Now, if you want to put to him that he knows what his brother was doing but won't discuss it, you can put it, but that will take only a few moments. So I leave it to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jusic, that on the 12th of October, 1991, your brother joined the Defence of the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in this first part, some 20 minutes ago, I told you that I hadn't at all seen my brother. I didn't at all see him during the war, so that I think that you are asking your question of the wrong party. I told you decidedly that I moved within the city of Dubrovnik walls and that there were no events of this kind or any similar events, so that this is the wrong address that you're addressing this question to. I really don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then please let your answer be, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it not the case that your brother was deployed in the area of the village of Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your brother was located throughout this period in the office building of the INA with other members of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This begs the question of whether you know where the INA building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, do you know this or do you not know this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is crazy. The INA building is quite the opposite side of the city, where the insurance building is. As to your question, I don't know, but your question is really not a proper one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll read this out for you. On page 3, the first, second, third -- fourth paragraph, where it is written the following. This is the statement of Mujica Jusic, father Arif, of the 27th and 31st of May, 2001. And it reads: "[In English] The next day we moved to a building that is 100 metres from the police headquarters (Today the building is the INA building.) That building became our base for 22 days. We slept there in the offices." [Interpretation] Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, this is what your brother had to say: [In English] "Several days later my unit consisting of myself and about four other guys was issued with a [Broing] Browning 12.7-millimetres heavy machine-gun." [Interpretation] Do you know that your brother was issued with a heavy machine-gun of the Browning type throughout October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I neither know what a Browning or Broing is, nor do I know of that particular bit of information. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate paragraph on the same page, page 3, he says: "[In English] The first war action that we were involved in whilst operating out of our base came only after the JNA had occupied Bosanka, Strincera, Zarkovica, and Golubov Kamen." [Interpretation] Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, sir, you know pitting these four or five soldiers again the entire Yugoslav army, that's really little. If they defended the hometown and the children, I take my hat off to them, and it really only increases my pride in them and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of your brother's statement: "[In English] We never really shot at a specific target, we just knew that the JNA were up the hill and we fired in their general direction. We would expand a complete charger then drive as fast as possible from the site where which we had fired. This was vital, as the JNA would return fire, with mortars, immediately at our firing position." [Interpretation] Is it not the case that the Croatian army was resorting to these particular tactics?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honey, I saw no soldiers of any kind. It is a good tactic now that I think about it. It is a sheer partisan tactic, the kind we were taught about in our school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, was it effective? Did it give results, this tactic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said yourself they were opening fire from this heavy machine-gun and the mortars responded, and I, even though an amateur, know that there is a huge difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "[In English] The positions that we fired from varied greatly. We had a practice of moving about two kilometres between firing points to confuse the JNA so they couldn't locate us or know precisely what our strength was." [Interpretation] Is this also an element of this good tactic of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is horrendous. One should shoot a movie about this. You just have five guys pitted against the entire Yugoslav army. I know nothing about it, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But if this is true, what your brother said to the investigators of the OTP, does it not mean that your brother and the five of them are heroes who defended, managed to defend Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. Once again I understand Mr. Petrovic's need to put the statement to the witness, of course if he intends to substantiate it by bringing Defence evidence in due course, but bearing in mind the witness's response to the first question in this line of questioning, namely that he didn't know that his brother was in the Croatian defence force of any nature whatsoever, it is a bit farfetched to ask the witness himself to speculate on the consequences of questions that Mr. Petrovic is putting to him, namely reading out elements of his brother's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will allow this question, Mr. Kaufman. He is not necessarily bound by an answer, as you would understand, and what he is raising here is whether or not his brother was in fact a hero of the Croatian army, and I think that is a matter that is of concern to the Defence and relevant to the trial and ought to be allowed to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I please have an answer?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my knowledge, my brother was not decorated for his valour, but in my eyes he is a hero now that you have given me this report of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Jusic, that this is the first time you hear about this, from me, 13 years later? Is it only now that you found out your brother is a hero?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my eyes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm the first person you found out about this from?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the first time I hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Further on in your brother's statement, it says: "[In English] Car park alongside the northern wall of the Old Town."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are clarifying the point that was a problem awhile ago. "[In English] During the first week of November 1991 we were sent to this location to shoot at the JNA who had been sighted next to the cross on Srdj. This was the same day that Hotel Imperijal was destroyed. This was the first time we used our Browning machine-gun." [Interpretation] In the next paragraph, your brother says: "[In English] We went from our base at INA down Ante Starcevic Street through Pile bus station and around to the northern wall of the Old Town. On arriving at this location we stopped at the entrance to the parking area alongside the city walls. At this the JNA were already shelling the area. I think the JNA may have seen us approaching as we were exposed as we drove down Ante Starcevic Street." [Interpretation] Do you know anything about this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. But really, you expect people to take their pants off, to put it in vulgar terms now, and to wait for the town to be razed. Well, good for them that they were engaged in this defence. I would have been engaged in the defence too if I had something in my hands. What happened was shameful. This client who you are defending here so nicely - and it's a good thing you're doing so - he forced me to sleep in a small hallway for a year and a half like a mouse in a hole because of your mortar shells and other shells. Talk about that for a while. That is shameful. I feel sorry for the gentleman, too. It's a tragedy. It's a shameful thing. But this shouldn't have happened at all. We shouldn't have been here at all. We could have been sitting in Dubrovnik or in Belgrade and living a peaceful life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed, Mr. Jusic. On page 5, paragraph 1 -- or, rather, the last sentence on page 4: "[In English] We drove the truck forwards about 30 metres or so, and one of our men (Nenad Vrankovic - now deceased) fired a short burst of fire from our machine-gun in the general direction of the JNA. We could not see anyone to shoot at, but we were ordered (via the radio) to open fire into the area immediately below the cross." [Interpretation] Did your brother's fire perhaps damage the cross?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was impossible. It was hit by a gunboat from the sea. The shooting went on for days, and as a matter of fact, they said later that it was a question of prestige which particular gunboat would destroy the cross. And these were enormous shells. I saw it on film later. I told you awhile ago that up there, there was no -- there were no JNA troops. I said that very specifically up there. There were no JNA troops by the cross, and it's about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see any reason why your brother along with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I'd ask the answer to be completed, if possible. There was an answer that was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I think it was finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But if not, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said everything I wanted to say, but I would like the transcript to reflect all of it, because it is nuances that are important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Montovjerna is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Montovjerna the right accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise because of my accent. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is on a hillock facing Gruz. Gruz is to the right, Lapad is to the left, and Montovjerna is between the two roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So on page 5, Montovjerna is the heading. Did I pronounce it right now?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bravo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] A couple of days after the event described above, we were told to spend the night up in the Montovjerna part of town. I do not know why we were sent there. We did as we were told but did not fire our weapon and did not come under the fire from the JNA. This was the only occasion that we were at this position." [Interpretation] In your walks around town or towards Lapad or perhaps when you went to the Libertas Hotel, did you go through that part of town which is called Montovjerna?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for that. That is a bit further up and roads go left and right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there were some troops there or did you not know about that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The same page: "[In English] Solitudo area of Babin Kuk peninsula. We were then sent here to provide cover fire for our men on the front line at Sustjepan." [Interpretation] Then your brother says that there was a bunker there, and so on and so forth. And then he says: "[In English] I think we took up this position around 20th November 1991, and we remained in this position up until May 1992." [Interpretation] Tell me, please, what is in the Solitudo area in Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vilas. That is also where the yachting club is called Orsan, and from that side, from the side of Solitudo, you can't really see Sustjepan because it's behind the hill, but that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far could one go through Dubrovnik? Was Sustjepan the western border, as far as one could go?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible to go there and there was no reason to go there. This is simply the road to Mokosica and out of Dubrovnik. As far as we know, on the other side of the river there were JNA positions. They were shooting from there, and they killed quite a few people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please let us move on to page 6 now of Mr. Mujica Jusic's statement: "[In English] I am aware that in addition to the Browning heavy machine-gun operated by my unit there were a number of other heavier weapons operated by the forces defending the city of Dubrovnik (during the period October to December 1991.) These weapons and their locations are as follows: "M20-1, 20-millimetre anti-aircraft cannon mounted on a truck. The M20-1 cannon was fitted with a box or magazine containing about 25 rounds. I can't recall who was in charge of operating this weapon. The unit was based in a building called Castle Pucic on Ante Starcevic Street just below the old hospital. I know that they were based there as sometimes we would meet up and they told us where they were based. I also recall that I heard of their location over our Motorola radios." [Interpretation] Did you see this three-barrelled gun that your brother is talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, it is at the address that you mentioned. That is where the Dubrovnik Symphony Orchestra is. I was not there every day but I was there at least once a week. I had rehearsals, and there was no gun there, not one that I saw, at any rate. No markings, no signs, no nothing. This is a beautiful Renaissance garden with palm trees and pine trees. And the door is a very narrow one. It is impossible to go through it. Perhaps only a very a small car could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see this three-barrelled gun that your brother refers to anywhere else in the street?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Debris is the only thing that could be seen in the streets and also the Imperijal Hotel burned down, and debris, burned trees, bricks, in the road. I cannot answer anything by way of what you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] M20-3, 20-millimetre anti-aircraft weapon, mounted on a truck. This was commanded by Milan Jejina. This weapon, with a maximum effective range around 500 to 1.600 metres was much more powerful than the M20-1 20-millimetres." [Interpretation] Let us move on as fast as possible. You probably didn't see these weapons either.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, but there is an answer I simply have to give you at this point. Dubrovnik is by the sea and Srdj is at least two kilometres up. So they could not do any shooting at all. I mean, even if they were shooting, it had no effect whatsoever. They were not like Sarajevo, in a valley. So it is impossible for them to have the proper kind of range. I'm not very knowledgeable about weapons, but this must be two kilometres away, and Zarkovica is even three kilometres away, so the weapons couldn't reach that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So even if they were shooting, it was to no avail.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you certainly didn't see them shooting or hear them shooting.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them or hear them shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, your brother says: "[In English] Mortars stationed at Babin Kuk. I do not know their calibre. The commander of this unit was ex-JNA officer named Bato Kovac." [Interpretation] Are there hotels there around the locality that your brother refers to?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Babin Kuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are hotels there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these hotels where refugees were put up?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Argos, Minceta, Dubrovnik President, Neptun. These are the names of the hotels that were full of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Paragraph 4: "[In English] Mortars stationed at Bogisica Park. I do not know their calibre. The crew operating these weapons would leave the weapons there but return every now and then to fire them." [Interpretation] Where is the Bogisica Park?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we call it a different way. Perhaps we use a different name for it. Is it Gradac, perhaps? Is that the park you're referring to? I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I simply cannot believe that you as a native of Dubrovnik confuse Bogisica Park and Gradac Park.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm confusing things, but quite a few addresses changed after the war. I know who Bogisic is, but I don't know exactly at this time where the Bogisic Park is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I've heard of Bogisic. We have some popular names for certain localities in Dubrovnik, so perhaps that's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your brother refers to it as Bogisic Park.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that's the official name but the people call it differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Anica Boskovic Street is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't think it's in town, though. It's not within the Old City walls, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the Imperijal Hotel is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly. Uz Vrtove is the name of the street behind the Imperijal Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell the Trial Chamber what the name of the park right behind the Imperijal Hotel is.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the Imperijal Hotel? We call that Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Any other names?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that what we're talking about right now?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's the Bogisic Park, but we've called it, from as far back as I can remember, Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something; how far away is Ilijina Glavica from Pile, from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a kilometre and a half, two at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The streets are winding, so it's hard for me to tell as the crow flies. If we're talking about the same place when we talk about Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the park behind the Imperijal Hotel.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind the hotel, further up, we call that Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is Ilijina Glavica farther away from Lapad -- farther away than Lapad?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is much closer than Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago you said to us that from your house there was two kilometres to Lapad.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is a straight road that goes to Lapad, whereas I told you that the streets going to Ilijina Glavica are very winding streets, so it's hard for me to tell exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how much is it as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 700 metres. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will the witness please be shown Exhibit D31.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this photograph and tell me, behind the Minceta, the points that you can see behind the Minceta, is this what you're referring to as Ilijina Glavica?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be, may be. It is not right behind the Minceta. It's a long way from the Minceta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We no longer need this photograph.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call this Ilijina Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Under item 5 -- but before that, please tell me, because there was some confusion between Bogisica Park and Gradac and Ilijina Glavica. Where is the Gradac Park?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is behind the radio station, behind the university centre which was burnt to the ground. It is right behind the Lovrijenac Fort, some 100 or 200 metres. It is on the seaside. The nun's cloister is there, a nunnery, then there is a hospital, an old hospital there, and the Libertas Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far is Gradac Park from, for instance, the Pile Gates or all the Bokar Gate or --

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bokara. Well, it is about 700 metres away. One needs to go into the centre and then to the left and you immediately reach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you take the road to Pile and just turn left and you are already at Gradac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is Gospino Polje?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gospino Polje is in the valley just under the Hotel Libertas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How far from the Libertas Hotel?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hundred or 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And under item 5 on page 6, your brother says: "[In English] A cannon (I do not know not the type) located in Gospino Polje. This cannon was operated by a guy called Jaksa (I do not know his other name). The targeting device on this cannon did not work and many people talked about the lack of accuracy of this weapon. To the best of my knowledge, he did not use this cannon until 6th December when he was tasked to help defend Srdj, but it was well known that some of his explosives landed long and others short of the target." [Interpretation] Have you heard about this cannon?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should have been a famous cannon, but I didn't hear about it. But let me just tell you this: Dubrovnik was surrounded, blockaded from air, from land, by planes, and from ships. When this official ship sailed out from Dubrovnik, the women and children who were allowed to leave Dubrovnik, it was checked -- intercepted and checked by the JNA in the channel and inspected. So I'm telling you this because there was no route through which weaponry could have entered Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you asserting that Dubrovnik was not supplied with arms either by sea or land routes prior to October?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly could not have been supplied by land. And as for the sea routes, I do know that all the ships were inspected and in fact some were taken to Zelenika in Montenegro for such searches. So I believe that it stands to reason that this was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your brother continues: "[In English] With reference to the mortars described above, I must add that prior to the 26th of November, 1991, these mortars were rarely used. "On 6 December 1991 ... the JNA launched their largest attack on the city of Dubrovnik. The attack started about 5.00 a.m. At this time our Browning machine-gun was stationed at Solitudo on the Babin Kuk peninsula ... We had spent the previous night in the house --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I would object there. There was, in my submission, a further element of that sentence, contained in brackets, that Mr. Petrovic decided not to read out because it inclines us to believe that there's a reference to the earlier use of the same sentence. If I could read the seen answer as it appears in my copy: "At this time our Browning machine-gun was stationed at Solitudo on the Babin Kuk peninsula (as described above)." "As described above" was the reference to the fact that the arm placed at Solitudo on the Babin Kuk peninsula was engaging Sustjepan. Your Honours, once again I have made my objection known to this line of questioning, bearing in mind that the witness has stated right at the start that he is not aware of the fact that his brother was a member of the Croatian defence forces, and I do hope that, bearing in mind this objection, if this line of questioning is to continue, that Mr. Petrovic, in due course, will be calling someone to substantiate these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is one of the bases upon which the questioning is being allowed to continue, Mr. Kaufman, and you have now got on record the concern that you were raising before the break as to what was actually said by the witness's brother in his statement. So if you'd carry on now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] We had spent the previous night in the house at that location. When the attack started, we went from the house to our weapon. "The first thing we noticed was the JNA tank moving from Strincera towards the Imperijal Fortress at the top of Srdj. "Looking towards Gruz port I saw a Greek boat that had brought humanitarian supplies hit by a JNA shell. The boat was damaged but managed to make its way out of the port area and out to sea. Many boats in the port were hit and sunk that day. "About 20 people, mostly civilians, were killed by the JNA shelling on that day. The JNA opened fire from many different directions, and their shells fell everywhere, on the Old Town, throughout the remainder of the city and on the Lapad and Babin Kuk peninsulas. "We monitored the course of the Croatian response to the JNA by listening to our Motorola radio. We heard one of the commanders (I cannot recall who that was) give the order for our mortar units to start shelling Srdj. When I heard that order, I knew things must have been getting bad for our men in Srdj Fort." [Interpretation] Do you wish me to read this through, Mr. Kaufman? Of course I'm prepared to do so, but there is a lot of it left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can do it in re-examination, but perhaps it would be helpful, Mr. Petrovic, if you could read the next sentence. It is quite appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] My unit did not fire any shots that day and we reminded [sic] in our position at Solitudo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: That's "remained."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe this is sufficient for a correct presentation? Did you hear, Mr. Jusic, these mortars of the Croatian army, according to the words of your brother, were issued orders already early that morning to open fire at JNA position?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really admire you, sir. I have admiration for you because several times you referred to the statement of my brother, and you said that he was alone with either four or five men with him. And as you go along you keep increasing the number eventually until it becomes a whole army. Is it not disgraceful? Is it not disgraceful for you to disgrace your own army when you had such a strong army armed to the teeth which was opposed by four or five lads, and now your are embellishing and embellishing your story until their number grows to hundreds and so on and so forth. You said before yourself there were just four or five lads. Having said this, I don't know anything about it, but this is just a statement I have to make. Please do not burden me with these considerations. What army are we talking about? I saw no army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, I believe that you have understood the fact that I am not doing the embellishing, it is your brother who you said was a decent man, a serious man of integrity who gave this statement to the same Prosecutor's office to which you have given your statement. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he said there were four of them and you are building a whole army out of it, adding the zeros as you go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that Mr. Jusic is defending himself very well on the witness stand, but once again I'd like to remind Mr. Petrovic there is no need to go into the integrity and decency of his brother, or at least put it to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. Mr. Petrovic, I am putting a different point, and that is that I think that you are -- have covered with extreme thoroughness this area but at a considerable cost of time, and I would encourage you now to move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your patience. I believe that you are satisfied with how important it was for me to present what I did. I only have another question in this particular connection and then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, did you hear about the 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying that perhaps there were 162 brigades? I never heard of it. And if there was a 163rd, there must have been the 1st, 2nd, and so on brigade, and I wouldn't have missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a Croatian army at all in the period that we are referring to, which is the fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I heard, there was an army in Vukovar, in Slavonia, in Split when the destroyers started opening fire at Split. It was a nascent army arising as a liberation, as a defence movement. But concretely speaking, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your brother, your brother Djurmane Mujica, what is he by profession?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an excellent drummer, drummer in a band, and he played for a long time at these hotels, at precisely these hotels that your people demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you kindly if I do my best to appreciate you, for you to show equal respect for me. When you say "your people," do you make a distinction, and if you do, please do make a distinction and treat the Defence in a courteous way, the way you treat the other parties and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a tone that you imposed, sir. Actually, I was just giving you a taste of your own medicine. I ask you to respect me and my brother and countless time I responded I don't know, I don't know, I don't know, and I also said that if my brother indeed did what you say he did, that I take my hat off to him as a defender of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know -- you didn't know that your brother was defender of Dubrovnik. Did you know anyone, anyone else who was?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew a lad. He was a really likable chap. His name was Mario Peci and he had a disco club at Lazarina. He was killed at Bosanka during the first days. But he was not in uniform. He was wearing a tracksuit and tennis shoes. And up there he was killed and another guy, another lad by the name of Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what were they doing on Bosanka?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an outing locality, the Bosanka site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said this is -- this is where you picnicked. At the risk of being cynical, were they there for an outing, for a picnic, or on any other business?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only information I gave you was that they got killed there by the JNA and that this, generally speaking, Zarkovica, Bosanka, this is a viewpoint, an outing locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And does that mean that these two men were members of the Defence of the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them defending. I didn't see any weapons. I know these were nice, likable guys. They would say hello to me, I would say hello to them. This was a successful guy, the owner of a discotheque. I had no other contacts with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of a man by the name of Nojko Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who is this man?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nojko Marinovic is an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, a Croat by nationality in terms of ethnic background, I believe, and he knew much more about these things that we're discussing today, much more than you know and much more than I know, and he was there to defend his Croatia. I don't know where he was positioned. I only know that his name was frequently referred to. In fact, I was once introduced to him. I believe it was 1997 or 1998. There was a promotion event for a book or something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak up and into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was it that you heard about this person that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I heard that they had some suspicions about him because he was from the JNA ranks, and I also heard that he was a very resourceful, a very adroit person, a tactical soldier. And I heard everything nice about him. And from this distance I respect what I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you heard that he was an adroit tactician. Where was -- who was he competing with in terms of tactics?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe with the attackers. You know who it was that attacked Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But as in Dubrovnik there were no army, there was no defence, there wasn't anything; how was he trying to outdo the attacker?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he sought to prevent them from attacking us to the extent that they were doing. I heard stories about this person as a very nice person, a very capable person, meaning that he had been educated and trained very well by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what was it that you heard about his tactical ability?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The finale showed it all, the finale being that the army did not -- the Yugoslav People's Army did not manage to completely destroy Dubrovnik and to enter Dubrovnik. And if this was his doing or, rather, to his credit, then he deserves every praise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But was he not the commander of the defence of the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said. That is what they wrote. Now, whether he was defending the city from Dubrovnik or from the surroundings, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you did not hear any of this until very recently. You didn't know it in 1991.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. The newspapers wrote about him. Our press is very open. People can write about all sorts of things. He was portrayed in the newspapers the way I had put it just now. And people talked about him too. They talked about him with admiration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me. Tell me anything. What were they saying about him?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that he was in Trebinje, that he had some kind of rank in the Yugoslav army, and that on one day when he saw this armada that was getting ready to go to Dubrovnik from Trebinje, that he as a Croat was offended by that and he crossed to the other side to organise the defence of Croatia. Stories went around about him just like the stories told about Kraljevic Marko in Serbia are. Let's put it that way. As a resourceful man, a capable man. And I admired him, too, through these stories. He came with nothing in his hands, but he did organise something, and the result is that we did indeed defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I see that you are very familiar with this man. What was it that you heard? With whose assistance did he achieve this colossal success?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, our entire town or our main street is like a living-room, as we put it. That is where ladies and gentlemen come and, let's put it this way, ordinary people too. And people chat, just like we're sitting here and talking. So everybody knows something, and then they add things to what other people are saying, so he becomes an imaginary hero. I first saw him three or four years ago, as I already said. He's a thin man, likable, nice looking. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us a legend about how Nojko Marinovic defended Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legend is that he came. When he came, his name meant something, because we had no one at our helm. I am a composer, another man is, say, a carpenter, whatever. So then he trained all these men, because Dubrovnik was not defended only from the east - and that's what we keep discussing here - it was attacked from the hinterland as well. I told you, I don't have any specific stories to tell about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he rally together musicians as well, some musicians?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. Not really, because at that time, I was the conductor of the symphony orchestra and also of the brass band. Often we went out, we were below the city walls, and we played music often. We often played the Liberty March, the American Liberty March, and that raised the morale of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your brother was a musician, a drummer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A good drummer at that, very talented. For a while, he played with me in the Trubidors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he have a job after 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be employed is a relative thing. Everything was destroyed and there was nowhere to work. We had a bakery that baked bread, and it was bombed 50 times, and somehow they managed to organise things and bake bread after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, from 1991 until today, was your brother employed somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which year this was, but he opened a shop, a store selling CDs, a music shop. He also sold instruments; guitars, mandolins, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your brother, from October 1991 until 1996 was in the 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, sir, we've already dealt with that question, and it would be a good thing for you to ask him about this. So please let us finish this subject now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: One more question: Is it really a fact that for five years you did not know what your own brother was doing and you expect us to believe that?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? My brother is about 45 or 50. Am I supposed to check on my brother, what he's doing and so on and so forth? That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I beg your pardon. Do you perhaps share my feeling that the time would be right for us to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was holding on, thinking you were about at the end of your cross-examination. I continue with these hopes, Mr. Petrovic. We will have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with Mr. Petrovic's leave, I'd just like to raise one small matter. I believe that Mr. Petrovic has now concluded this particular section of his questioning, the questioning with respect to the statement of the witness's brother. As is appropriate, I would submit in such circumstances, I feel it important that it be stated for the record that this was a statement taken on a certain date, and that is the 27th and 31st of May, 2001, whereas the witness's statement was taken in September, 23rd of September and 29th of September, 2000. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, please be so kind as to tell me what is a -- or, rather, the Crisis Staff in Dubrovnik in October to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was mainly concerned, to the best of my knowledge, with the protection of cultural monuments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the Crisis Staff were?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself was a member. I was in charge of culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a -- another musician, a critic, and his name was -- I cannot recall his name now. I can see his face in front of me. Perhaps I can -- I will remember later, if you can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot recall his name really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who appointed you to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one asked me whether I wanted to be a member. I was just told, "You are a member of the Crisis Staff," and I have this letter stating so. There were four or five members of us. There were musicians on the staff, there was a reviewer, a critic. I cannot remember all the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who sent you this letter?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this memorandum was sent us by the city council of the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who is the president of the city council?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now or then?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then, of course.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the name of the president was Mr. Sikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is his first name Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps not the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember these things. I was in touch with him, I can relate -- I can tell you on what occasions I got in touch with him if you're interested. In 1991, on New Year's Eve, there was organised, through the offices of the French government, more precisely Mr. Kouchner, a concert in Dubrovnik, and this concert was held. Participating in it was an orchestra from Lyon, France. The famous American singer Barbara Hendrix was also there. I was there with my children's choir as well, and there was a trumpet player, a soloist, I believe. Great artists from all over the world came to the concert. For instance, the greatest director of Great Britain, Peter Brooke; Michel Piccoli, the famous French actor also came. They came aboard a vessel to Dubrovnik, and the concert was held at midnight at the Franciscan cloister and was televised live by -- on Eurovision. After the concert ended, an hour and a half after the end, they departed by ship again. This is one of the roles of the Crisis Staff that I can now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How often did you meet?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. We never met. I mean, we never had meetings of the four or five of us. Never. This was an occasion on which we gathered and Mr. Zeljko asked me, as an expert on music, whether this was all right, whether this or that in connection with this was okay, and in fact I insisted that this concert be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the members of the Crisis Staff were people in charge of either music or architecture, others again for town planning, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you say their president was Zeljko Sikic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I believe he was. It seems to me that he was. I saw him often in Dubrovnik, and we communicated mainly in the street. We ran across each other in the street. I never had any reason to go to see him in his office except this one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And this one time in connection with this concert on New Year's Eve?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in connection with this concert on New Year's Eve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you never met as a member of the Crisis Staff with other members of the Crisis Staff throughout this period October to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether these other members of the Crisis Staff, Zeljko Sikic and the others, whether they met?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe they had any reason to meet, and if there was a meeting, I don't see why I wouldn't have been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you be so kind as to tell us how did this Crisis Staff function at all if nobody ever met with no one but you just happened to meet, to run into one another in the street?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was more for show, so to speak. I didn't need any advice as to what I was doing. There was no need for them to meet with me to advise me on my particular line of activity. Whether the others met, I don't know. I did my civic duty to provide some impetus to the cultural life in the city, and I did that with success.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did the Crisis Staff perhaps not deal with issues of defence of the city?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did not the Crisis Staff perhaps concern itself with the questions of police in the town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police was on the opposite end of the city. We had nothing whatsoever to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did not perhaps the Crisis Staff see to the supply of the town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For instance, I myself was on one occasion, and I just now remember, I was on duty handling two telephones. People were calling from the island, saying there were some attacks. People were calling from the Zupa, saying that there were some movements of troops. But with these two telephones I could only acknowledge this fact, take note of events that were going on, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were you on this duty?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Meaning by the Rector's palace in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The address is in front of the palace, number 1, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two hours, and this was just on this -- on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who then replaced you? Who took over?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One young man came, I know, because I was scared to death because I had to go home at 2.00 a.m., after midnight, and it was the curfew. So this was imprinted in my memory as a scene from Bergman's films.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know a person, a gentleman by the name of Mato Valjalo?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know one Valjalo, but I believe this is a deceased person, a colleague of yours, a jurist. If that's the one that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mato Valjalo who was the driver of the chief of the Crisis Staff Zeljko Sikic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now I know. He was here recently. He told me that he was going to The Hague, but I confused him with this other person. He has a moustache, and he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who told you to stand duty, to be on duty in the city hall, in the Crisis Staff in the city hall?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am unable to respond to that question. I can't recall. I know -- I only know that I did this, performed this as a civic duty, as a citizen who was obliged to do it without, of course, if you're interested, any weaponry or anything else. I didn't even have a glass of water in front of me like you do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: As you were on duty minding the telephone, who was it that you were supposed to report to if someone reported anything of interest to you?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a vent, so to speak, for the citizens, just to have someone to call, someone to talk to. "Officer on duty, person on duty, are you there? I can sight a ship moving about near town." Or from the Zupa someone would report some movements, troops moving towards Dubrovnik, tanks moving toward Dubrovnik. So this was actually a device whereby the citizens could vent their concerns of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And these reports that you received via the telephone from people, did you jot that down anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no one to report this to nor did I have reason to jot it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And if a ship was moving, a warship, a battleship, as at from Jeta [phoen] moving through the channel, you reported that to no one?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was sort of a ruse. It was a game of sorts. It was easier for people if they knew there was a person they could report such things to because I would tell them, "Fear not, we are here," and I would apply all my dramatic devices in order to assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What would you tell them?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would tell them, "Never fear. We are here. There is nothing they can do to us. We shall overcome," and the like. It was all really innocuous. It was like a child's game. You know, everyone was deceiving the other person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you say so, I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me. It was pure Ionesco [UNESCO].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Djuro Korda?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I think that should be Ionesco, the playwright, not "UNESCO." A comedy of the absurd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretationi] Yes, I said Ionesco.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am much more prosaic in my questions. I'm not talking about this, I'm asking you about Djuro Korda.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was referring to the absurdity of the situation and I referred to it being a Ionesc one. Can I tell you who Djuro Korda is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I don't know Djuro. I know Luka Korda. He was the president, and he was -- he is -- he was a man number one in Konavle. I don't know Djuro Korda. I know Luka Korda personally. He is a very nice, likable person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was he perhaps not the president of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luka Korda was the president of the HDZ. I can remember that. That was in Konavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was his brother Djuro perhaps the chief of the police department in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was not. I don't know. This is not my milieu. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Nikola Obuljen is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ex-mayor of Dubrovnik and a personal friend of mine. He was a negotiator during the war, in fact. He often went to Montenegro for negotiations. They would negotiate when they came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. He may have been. Perhaps he was even the president, but don't take my word for it. I'm not sure. Don't try to actually catch me in it, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you often discuss the situation with Obuljen in that period?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that period we only saw each other infrequently. When they returned by vessel from Cavtat or wherever it is that they went for negotiations, but later we were often together. He holds my art in high esteem, and he was a very good mayor too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever mention, I mean Mr. Obuljen, having negotiated with Admiral Jokic, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here, in our town, the city -- the name which was the name most referred to, the most often mentioned was that of the respected Mr. Jokic and Mr. Zec, and a certain Brzk [phoen]. I don't -- I don't know -- I cannot recall the name of this person. They were in graffiti on the walls. The name which was most often mentioned was Sofronije. I don't know what rank this man held. I only saw him once when the first shell landed in Dubrovnik, and he was wearing a uniform. This is the name most often mentioned in Dubrovnik, of the military names, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Obuljen tell you something about how the negotiations were developing?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not mention any names, but he always came back with lots of optimism. However, what he would talk about would not actually happen. Sometimes when they came back -- it's not that he went on his own, he went with other people too. They would hardly come back and the shooting would resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Miso Mihocevic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well. He was interpreter during those negotiations. When there would be some kind of international negotiation he went with them, with Obuljen, then there was Djuro Kolic on the team too, and I don't know who else went to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Miso was together with Kolic Obuljen?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the official interpreter, because there were always some foreigners present during the negotiations; UN people, observers, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, he was the official interpreter of the Dubrovnik delegation?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever see any of the persons I mentioned just now in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Sofronije. He was the only one who entered town. And also the soldiers above my house, as I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the people from Dubrovnik? Did you ever see any one of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Recently there was a film on television, on Belgrade television, a really good film produced by TV B92.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to tell you that on this film you can see very nicely that they were not wearing uniforms. That's the only thing I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Any -- what about these people that we mentioned from Dubrovnik, the ones that we talked about over the past few minutes? Did they have anything to do with the army?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that Obuljen, as a member of the Crisis Staff, negotiated on behalf of the Crisis Staff, or did he do it on somebody else's behalf?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, he is a prominent citizen, and I think that the citizens -- had the citizens had their choice in terms of who would negotiate in their name, they would have wanted Obuljen. I would be the first to do so because he's a very spirited politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know who Pero Poljanic is?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pero Poljanic was the mayor of Dubrovnik then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's your relationship with Mr. Poljanic?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. We say hello to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you pleased by the way he ran the town at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing much to say, but what I held against him was that he never addressed the citizens of Dubrovnik over the radio, for example, as opposed to, say, the bishop and other politicians at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since you know all these people, some of them more, some of them less, were there any conflicts between Sikic and Obuljen on one side and Poljanic on the other side? For example, regarding their general concept, how to defend oneself and what to do with regard to the situation?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That kind of thing was not obvious if that's what you're after.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear of the initiative to demilitarise the town of Dubrovnik that was launched by the top authorities of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, this did not really have to take place, this kind of action, because the town had been demilitarised. There was no army there. So there was nothing to be disarmed and no uniforms to be taken off when there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you not heard of the initiative at all or was there nothing to demilitarise?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about this term demilitarisation, I reject it. There was this initiative in the field of culture as Dubrovnik was being demolished that all the treasures of St. Blaise Church and other artworks should be transferred to Italy. That's the only kind of initiative I heard of. And I remember signing that initiative that that should be done, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you did not hear that the mayor of Dubrovnik, the president of the Executive Council of Dubrovnik sent a letter to the leadership, asking that Dubrovnik be proclaimed a demilitarised town, that the armed conflicts stop?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. That was the wish of the entire world. I can only welcome that, as I did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not precise enough. To demilitarise the town, to have UN forces come into town. Do you know of such an initiative of the local authorities in the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know of a negative initiative that was launched by Mr. Kouchner, because he was, I don't know what, president of Medicins Sans Frontieres. I think that was the name. And he had a -- he held a lecture. I even attended. He brought a French warship so that the people of Dubrovnik could move out of Dubrovnik and then that Dubrovnik could be won through negotiations, and Dubrovnik had not been lost at all. And then people booed him out, and women said that that would not be the way to deal with it, rather, the other way around. So that was a decisive moment. This was such a stupid idea, and it was totally against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that Kouchner came to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said. I heard that's what he said, because I put a counter-question to him: Is there perhaps a small footpath for us to return? He brought an enormous ship along, and many women and children took that boat to Venice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood all of this, you talked to Kouchner.

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended his lecture, and I was in the audience, and after the lecture he was taking questions from the audience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who was officially negotiating with Kouchner?

utterances.speaker: DJELO JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the stage there was another Frenchman, a philosopher. Then there was a gentleman called Mr. Demistura. I don't know who represented. And from Dubrovnik there was no one, really, with them. When these eminent people from the world came - eminent for want of a better word - people would come to hear their lectures but it wasn't that they were all that useful, these lectures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out that the ambassadors from 15 countries came?
